title: Arjuna drops his bow
hookLine: on the battlefield, Arjuna sinks down in despair

lines: DRIVE ME OUT. LET ME SEE.
cards: Conch shells blow. Two armies face each other on a wide field called Kurukshetra. A chariot rolls out between them, carrying the archer Arjuna, with his friend Krishna holding the reins.
Arjuna asked for this: drive me out, let me see who I'm fighting. And he looks across the field and sees the faces. Not strangers.
His teachers. Grandfathers. Cousins, uncles, friends.
The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture set inside the epic Mahabharata, begins right here, with a hero falling apart.

teach.b: First, the body. The Gita doesn't make Arjuna's despair noble or tidy. It makes it physical.
His limbs give way, he says, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles, his hair stands on end. His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and his skin burns. He can't stand; his mind is reeling.
What good is a kingdom won by killing the people I love? I don't want victory, or pleasures, or a throne, if this is the price. His argument is serious, and the text lets him make all of it.
At the end of the first chapter, Arjuna casts away his bow and arrows and sinks onto the chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
At the start of the second, he tells Krishna plainly, I will not fight, and falls silent. Tradition names the whole first chapter for his despair. Fourth, why it matters.
All of Krishna's teaching comes after this collapse, and in answer to it.

Tradition says Krishna here is God, teaching his friend; some readers also hear the battle as the struggle inside any person. Either way, the conversation doesn't begin while Arjuna is pretending to be fine.
It begins when he puts the bow down and admits he doesn't know what to do. The text opens its wisdom to a person in despair, not to one who has it together.

how: The Bhagavad Gita is read and recited at home, in temples and in study groups, and its first chapter, Arjuna's despair, is heard as the opening that makes the teaching possible.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you asked to see the enemy, and you see your teachers and cousins. your bow is in your hand. what do you do?
o: put the bow down and sink onto the chariot seat.
turn the chariot and ride home.
games.why: he casts away bow and arrows and sits, his mind overwhelmed with grief. the whole Gita grows from that moment.

practice: Let the body settle into the seat, the way Arjuna sank onto his, and admit silently one despair, one thing you don't know how to face.
Say it plainly to yourself, I don't know what to do about this, and feel what the body does: maybe a tightening, maybe a little release. You don't need an answer yet; Arjuna didn't have one either.

wordCard.voice: Gandiva, Arjuna's bow in the Gita, slips from his hand as despair overtakes him before Krishna's teaching begins. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: despair, dejection; tradition names the Gita's first chapter for Arjuna's viṣāda.

carryVoice: Your line: dropped the bow. Krishna's teaching began there, with the bow down, not before. See you tomorrow.
